In this post, I outline some simple micro-optimisations to be wary of when involved with large data-intensive tooling. Measurements stated here are automated and produced by the script, [`bin/benchmarks.py`](https://github.com/AnvarAtayev/anvaratayev.github.io/blob/main/bin/benchmarks.py).

# Speed

## Membership test: `set` vs `list` {#membership}

A set lookup is O(1); a list scan is O(n). Here `x = 999` is the worst case - the last element of the list.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
lst = list(range(1000)); st = set(lst); x = 999

# x in st
x in st

# x in lst
x in lst
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `x in st` | 16.5 ns/op | 1.0× |
| `x in lst` | 7.58 µs/op | 459× |

</div>

## Dict lookup with a default (key missing) {#dict-default-miss}

The same three patterns as [the hit case](#dict-default), but now the key is absent. `try/except` goes from cheapest to worst by far: raising and catching `KeyError` creates, propagates, and discards an exception object every time. `d.get` costs the same whether it hits or misses, and the `in` check gets *cheaper*.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
d = {'k': 1}

# try/except
try:
    v = d['missing']
except KeyError:
    v = 0

# d.get
v = d.get('missing', 0)

# in check
v = d['missing'] if 'missing' in d else 0
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `try/except` | 94.0 ns/op | 8.2× |
| `d.get` | 16.5 ns/op | 1.4× |
| `in check` | 11.4 ns/op | 1.0× |

</div>

## Converting a tuple to a list {#tuple-to-list}

`[*tup]` and `list(tup)` copy the underlying pointer array in C; the comprehension pushes every element through the bytecode loop.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
tup = tuple(range(1000))

# [*tup]
[*tup]

# list(tup)
list(tup)

# comprehension
[x for x in tup]
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `[*tup]` | 1.17 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `list(tup)` | 1.18 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `comprehension` | 7.60 µs/op | 6.5× |

</div>

## Building a string: `join` vs `+=` {#string-building}

`join` makes one pass over the parts; `+=` re-copies the growing string on every iteration.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
parts = ['abc'] * 1000

# ''.join
''.join(parts)

# += loop
s = ''
for p in parts:
    s += p
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `''.join` | 5.02 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `+= loop` | 31.41 µs/op | 6.3× |

</div>

## Summing: builtin `sum` vs manual loop {#builtin-sum}

The builtin iterates in C, skipping bytecode dispatch per element.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
data = list(range(1000))

# sum(data)
sum(data)

# manual loop
total = 0
for x in data:
    total += x
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `sum(data)` | 2.36 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `manual loop` | 11.72 µs/op | 5.0× |

</div>

## Queue from the front: `deque` vs `list` {#queue-front}

`deque.popleft` is O(1); `list.pop(0)` shifts every remaining element.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
from collections import deque; rng = range(1000)

# deque.popleft
d = deque(rng)
while d:
    d.popleft()

# list.pop(0)
l = list(rng)
while l:
    l.pop(0)
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `deque.popleft` | 21.39 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `list.pop(0)` | 75.05 µs/op | 3.5× |

</div>

## Squaring: `x*x` vs `x**2` {#power}

Exponentiation goes through the generic power protocol; plain multiplication does not.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
# x*x (int)
x = 42
x*x

# x**2 (int)
x = 42
x**2

# x*x (float)
x = 42.5
x*x

# x**2 (float)
x = 42.5
x**2
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `x*x (int)` | 11.7 ns/op | 1.1× |
| `x**2 (int)` | 17.8 ns/op | 1.7× |
| `x*x (float)` | 10.6 ns/op | 1.0× |
| `x**2 (float)` | 29.7 ns/op | 2.8× |

</div>

## Checking for `None`: `is` vs `==` {#none-check}

`is` is a single pointer comparison; `==` dispatches through the `__eq__` protocol.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
x = None

# x is None
x is None

# x == None
x == None

# not x
not x
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `x is None` | 5.4 ns/op | 1.1× |
| `x == None` | 9.1 ns/op | 1.9× |
| `not x` | 4.9 ns/op | 1.0× |

</div>

## Dict lookup with a default {#dict-default}

The key is present here, so `try/except` costs nothing; the `in` check looks up the key twice, and `d.get` costs a method call. The ranking inverts when the key is absent - see [the miss case](#dict-default-miss).

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
d = {'k': 1}

# try/except
try:
    v = d['k']
except KeyError:
    v = 0

# d.get
v = d.get('k', 0)

# in check
v = d['k'] if 'k' in d else 0
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `try/except` | 11.6 ns/op | 1.0× |
| `d.get` | 16.7 ns/op | 1.4× |
| `in check` | 19.7 ns/op | 1.7× |

</div>

## String formatting {#string-formatting}

f-strings are compiled to dedicated bytecode; `%` and `.format` go through runtime parsing or a method call.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
name = 'x'; val = 42

# f-string
f'{name}: {val}'

# % operator
'%s: %d' % (name, val)

# .format
'{}: {}'.format(name, val)
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `f-string` | 70.8 ns/op | 1.0× |
| `% operator` | 94.3 ns/op | 1.3× |
| `.format` | 117.2 ns/op | 1.7× |

</div>

## Building a list: comprehension vs `append` {#list-building}

Comprehension runs on a specialised bytecode path; the loop costs a method call per element.

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
data = list(range(1000))

# comprehension
out = [x for x in data]

# append hoisted
out = []
append = out.append
for x in data:
    append(x)

# append loop
out = []
for x in data:
    out.append(x)
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `comprehension` | 7.68 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `append hoisted` | 12.33 µs/op | 1.6× |
| `append loop` | 10.85 µs/op | 1.4× |

</div>

## `join`: list comprehension vs generator {#join-listcomp}

`str.join` needs two passes, it first drains a generator into a list - handing it a list comprehension skips the per-element `next()` calls. This is the speed side of the trade-off in [the memory comparison](#gen-vs-list).

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
seq = list(range(1000))

# list comp
''.join([str(x) for x in seq])

# generator
''.join(str(x) for x in seq)
```

| variant | time | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `list comp` | 45.77 µs/op | 1.0× |
| `generator` | 56.82 µs/op | 1.2× |

</div>

# Memory

## Generator vs list {#gen-vs-list}

Both compute the same sum, but the list comprehension materialises all 100,000 intermediate values before summing, while the generator holds one element at a time. (The list version is typically slightly faster - this is a speed/memory trade-off.)

<div class="bench-pair">

```python
# generator
total = sum(x*x for x in range(100_000))

# list comp
total = sum([x*x for x in range(100_000)])
```

| variant | peak memory | relative |
|---|---:|---:|
| `generator` | 728 B | 1.0× |
| `list comp` | 3.8 MiB | 5,496× |

</div>
